assignments.title: VR Activity: A Map Drawn Far Away
assignments.html:
VR ACTIVITY
A Map Drawn Far Away
Solo · one in-headset session
16 points · file upload or text entry
✺ ✦ ✺
Before you start

Finish both lessons and read both sources first. Your notes from each page are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the page, so open it before you write. Then write your answers and submit them in this assignment.

WHAT YOU'RE DOING

In 1884 and 1885 diplomats met in Berlin, without any African present, and set the rules for dividing a continent. In your VR headset you will walk across a large map of Africa as it stood in 1870 and again as it stood in 1914. Your task is to find evidence in the map for how the division happened and whose choices it left out.

WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset, charged and ready
▶
Your course page for this week, which lists the session link and the place to enter
▶
A notebook or open document for quick notes while you are in the session
▶
About 45 minutes in one sitting
HOW TO JOIN
Where to go: Open your immersive session from the link on your course page, then enter the location named there.
Solo or group: Solo. You do not need a partner.
If something fails: Write down what happened and use the help contact on your course page. Do not skip the activity.
WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Review first. Reread the sections of the lesson “The Scramble for Africa and the Raj” called The Scramble for Africa and African Resistance and British Ambition. Remember that the Berlin Conference included no Africans, that the borders were drawn on maps in Europe, and that Ethiopia and Liberia kept their independence.
2
Start in 1870. Stand on the map as it was in 1870. Note where Europeans held land and where they held almost none.
3
Walk to 1914. Move to the map of 1914 and walk across the continent. Pay attention to the shape of the borders. Notice which ones run in straight lines and which follow rivers or coasts.
4
Stop at three places. Choose three spots that help explain how or why the division happened. Good choices include the Congo, Fashoda, Omdurman, Adwa, or the Cape to Cairo route. At each one, capture a picture with your headset and jot a note about what you see.
5
Look for the people. At each spot, ask who is missing from the map. Think about the African rulers, soldiers, clerks, and workers that you read about, and what choices they made.
6
Write your response. After you leave the session, write one paragraph of about 150 to 200 words that answers this question: What does the map show about how Europeans divided Africa, and what can a map never tell you about the people who lived there?
WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit your three captured images and your paragraph in the Canvas assignment. Use the images as evidence in your writing, and name which picture you are referring to.

Estimated time: 45 minutes

SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I looked at the map as it was in 1870 and as it was in 1914.
☐
I captured three images that show different parts of the map.
☐
My paragraph uses at least two of my images as evidence.
☐
My paragraph connects what I saw to what I read about the scramble for Africa in the lesson “The Scramble for Africa and the Raj”.
☐
I wrote in complete sentences and kept to about 150 to 200 words.
FACILITATOR NOTE

Teacher-facing. Before releasing this activity, add the session link and the specific location to the course page, and confirm that students have a way to capture images in their headsets. The instructions above assume a room-scale or walkable map of Africa that shows both 1870 and 1914. If none is available, substitute another walkable map of the same period, such as a map of the British Raj and its railways, and adjust the steps and review section to match, and note the substitution in the teacher's manual. The instructions are platform-neutral on purpose. Grade with the course rubric for VR activities: three images as evidence, a paragraph that cites them, and reasoning tied to the lesson.

quizzes.title: Module Intro: Imperialism
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
Imperialism
2 questions · survey · one attempt
✺ ✦ ✺
Essential question for this week
What drove European powers to seize or pressure other lands, and how did Africans, Indians, Chinese, and Japanese respond?
Instructions

Welcome to Imperialism. This short check-in is not graded. Your answers help your teacher see where each student is starting, so answer honestly.

What you will be able to do

The Scramble for Africa and the Raj

  • Describe how European powers divided Africa between 1880 and 1900.
  • Explain how Britain came to rule India and how the Raj was governed.
  • Evaluate how technology, rivalry, and African and Indian choices shaped the outcome.

China and Japan: Opium, Unequal Treaties, and the Meiji Restoration

  • Describe how the opium trade led to war and unequal treaties in China.
  • Explain how Commodore Perry's visit set off the Meiji Restoration in Japan.
  • Evaluate why Japan reformed quickly while China struggled to do so.

discussions.title: Discussion: Was Imperialism About Profit, Power, or Duty?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Was Imperialism About Profit, Power, or Duty?
Imperialism
10 points · threaded discussion
✺ ✦ ✺
Before you start

Finish both lessons first. Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you post. Then post your answer here and reply to one classmate.

DISCUSSION PROMPT

Merchants wanted markets and raw materials. Governments wanted naval bases and prestige. Missionaries and humanitarians wanted to spread the Gospel and to end the slave trade. The lessons also show Africans, Indians, Chinese, and Japanese making choices of their own, and they show Leopold's Congo and the opium trade.

Take a position. Was imperialism mainly about profit, power, or duty? Support your position with at least two specific details from the lessons, and include one detail that points the other way. Explain why you weigh the evidence as you do.

Aim for about 150 to 200 words.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a detail from the lessons that they did not use. If not, explain respectfully where it falls short, and point to a detail from the lessons that supports your view.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
Criteria Substantive (full credit) Thin (partial credit) Missing (no credit)
Claim and evidence
5 pts		 Takes a clear position, supports it with at least two specific details from the lessons, and deals fairly with a detail that points the other way. Takes a position but gives only one detail, or stays general, or ignores the opposing detail. No post, or no clear position.
Response to a classmate
5 pts		 Answers a specific point in a classmate's post and either strengthens it with a new detail or explains politely where it falls short. Replies in general terms, such as agreeing or disagreeing without a detail from the lessons. No reply.
10 pts total
